section_1a.directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements below is followed by four suggested answers or completions. Select the one that is best in each case. You have 55 minutes.

questions.stimulus: In John Ford's 1939 Western Stagecoach, a stagecoach crosses dangerous Apache territory carrying a mixed group of passengers: a drunken doctor, a gambler, a prostitute, a timid whiskey salesman, and a proper banker's wife. The outlaw Ringo Kid joins them, seeking revenge on the men who framed him. The film's last line, spoken as the hero and heroine ride beyond the reach of the town's corrupt sheriff and respectable hypocrites: 'Well -- they're saved from the blessings of civilization.'
questions.stem: In a 1939 film set in 1885, a character says the hero and heroine are 'saved from the blessings of civilization' as they flee the reach of corrupt lawmen. What irony does this sarcastic usage highlight?
options: (A) Civilization always brings genuine freedom
(B) The frontier had no law or institutions at all
(C) The character sincerely praises the blessings of the legal system
(D) So-called civilized institutions can be corrupt

questions.stimulus:
Source 1: It goes without saying that in that event the U.S. government cannot fail to call to stern account those immediately responsible for the deliberate violation of the Soviet Union's national frontiers by American planes. It is natural that under these conditions we are unable to work at the conference, unable to work at it because we see from what positions it is desired to talk to us, under threat of aggressive intelligence flights. Everyone knows that spying flights are undertaken for intelligence purposes with a view to starting war. Accordingly, we reject the conditions in which the United States is placing us. We wish to be rightly understood by the peoples of all countries of the globe, by public opinion. The Soviet government is profoundly convinced that if not this U.S. government, then another, and if not another, then a third, will understand that there is no other solution than peaceful co-existence of the two systems, the capitalist and the socialist.

Source: Nikita Khrushchev, Summit Conference Statement, May 16, 1960

Source 2: At this morning's private session, despite the violence and inaccuracy of Mr. Khrushchev's statements, I replied to him in the following terms: the position of the United States was made clear with respect to the distasteful necessity of espionage activities in a world where nations distrust each other's intentions. We pointed out that these activities had no aggressive intent but rather were to assure the safety of the United States and the free world against surprise attack by a power which boasts of its ability to devastate the United States and other countries by missiles armed with atomic warheads.

Source: Dwight Eisenhower, Summit Conference Statement, May 16, 1960
questions.stem: Khrushchev's doctrine of 'peaceful co-existence' is most significant as which of the following?
options: (A) It continued Stalin-era Soviet doctrine without any real change.
(B) It meant the Soviet Union was abandoning socialism altogether.
(C) It broke with the Stalin-era assumption that capitalist-socialist war was inevitable.
(D) It was immediately rejected by all subsequent Soviet leaders after Khrushchev's fall.

questions.stimulus:
...it is not unreasonable to conclude that the Japanese and Korean peoples formed for a long time one and the same nation. The recent annexation of Korea by Japan is therefore not the incorporation of two different countries inhabited by different races, but, it may rather be said to be the reunion of two sections of the one and same nation after a long period of separation. Indeed it is nothing more nor less than the old state of things restored.... In developing the industry of an infantile nation, it is advisable to begin the work by undertaking the improvement of the agricultural industry, and this has been diligently carried on since Japan assumed the protectorate of the Korean Empire.

Source: Komatsu Midori, 'The Old People and the New Government,' in Transactions of the Korea Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1912
questions.stem: The author's claim that the annexation was 'nothing more nor less than the old state of things restored' was most likely intended to
options: (A) Document Korean resistance to the Japanese annexation of Korea.
(B) Call for the restoration of Korean independence from Japan.
(C) Criticize Japan's agricultural policies in Korea as exploitative.
(D) Persuade Western readers that Japan's rule over Korea was natural and beneficial.

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Daniel Boorstin, The Discoverers (1983): Within decades of Columbus's voyages, the European world was transformed. The dominant Island of the Earth, the connected landmass of Afro-Eurasia, was displaced by a dominant Ocean of the Earth, the connected body of water covering most of the surface. Never had the arena of human experience been so suddenly revised.
questions.stem: Mercantilists believed a nation must export more than it imports. Why?
options: (A) Imports are more valuable than exports because they bring desirable foreign goods home
(B) Gold and silver are worthless
(C) Trade policy does not matter
(D) Trade surpluses would be paid in gold and silver, the measure of power

questions.stimulus: For one of the world's societies to achieve global hegemony, it would have to enormously increase its productivity — a great leap accomplished before the scientific, technological, agricultural, and industrial revolutions on which our modern world rests. Such a leap could only be made by exploiting the ecosystems, mineral resources, and human labor of whole continents outside the lands of the society making it. Western Europe did just that, by means of its brutality and guns and, more important, by geographical and ecological luck. — Alfred Crosby, historian, Ecological Imperialism, 2004
questions.stem: Which of the following would provide the strongest evidence for Crosby's claim about Europe's 'geographical and ecological luck'?
options: (A) The catastrophic impact of Afro-Eurasian diseases on Native American populations.
(B) The outbreak of the Protestant Reformation.
(C) The invention of the printing press.
(D) The rise of powerful absolute monarchies in France and Spain during the 1500s and 1600s.

questions.stimulus: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, crossed the Sahara to Mecca on the hajj with a caravan carrying vast quantities of gold. On his return he built mosques and brought Muslim scholars to Mali. Decades later, the traveler Ibn Battuta found the people of Mali eager to memorize the Quran, while griots still recited the deeds of pre-Islamic kings at court.
questions.stem: Which statement about the spread of Islam in West Africa is best supported by the passage?
options: (A) Islam spread through Mali mainly by military campaigns of forced conversion that wiped out older beliefs and replaced them with Islamic law.
(B) Malian rulers rejected Islam entirely in order to preserve traditional religion.
(C) Trans-Saharan trade and royal patronage carried Islam into Mali's elite and urban culture, while older customs continued alongside it.
(D) West Africa had become fully Islamic long before any trans-Saharan trade existed.

questions.stimulus: The Tokugawa shogunate formalized the shi-no-ko-sho hierarchy: warriors (shi) ranked first, followed by peasants (no), artisans (ko), and merchants (sho) at the bottom — even though successful merchants often grew wealthier than the samurai above them.
questions.stem: Which of the following arguments about Tokugawa social order is best supported by the shi-no-ko-sho hierarchy?
options: (A) Tokugawa Japan was a fully commercialized society in which accumulated wealth alone determined a person's official status and rank.
(B) The hierarchy abolished the samurai class and replaced it with a merchant oligarchy.
(C) Peasants enjoyed the highest prestige in Tokugawa society because they produced the rice tax.
(D) The shogunate froze social ranks to preserve samurai dominance and keep merchants' wealth from becoming political power.

questions.stimulus: The frieze, carved in the centuries after Alexander's conquests, depicts the Buddha with deeply folded Greco-Roman drapery, a naturalistic body stance, and wavy hair tied in a Greco-style topknot — yet the subject is unmistakably the Buddha, seated among Indian devotees.
questions.stem: A stone frieze from Gandhara (in modern Pakistan) shows the Buddha carved with flowing Greek-style robes and a naturalistic stance borrowed from Hellenistic sculpture. What does this best illustrate about Hellenistic cultural exchange?
options: (A) The Greeks imposed their religion on India
(B) Indians had no artistic traditions before the Greeks arrived
(C) Alexander banned all local art forms
(D) Conquered peoples adapted Greek artistic forms to their own religious purposes

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of the Qianlong emperor's 1793 reply to King George III's embassy seeking expanded trade: Strange and costly objects do not interest me. Your tribute offerings are accepted only in recognition of the loyal spirit that sent them from afar. As your ambassador has seen, we possess all things; I set no value on curious or ingenious objects and have no use for your country's manufactures. Show still greater devotion and loyalty hereafter, so that by perpetual submission to our throne you may secure peace and prosperity.
questions.stem: Qianlong treats the British embassy as a tribute mission and lectures George III on future loyalty. What does this reveal about the Qing worldview?
options: (A) The Qing court feared British power
(B) The emperor desperately wanted British manufactures and pleaded for expanded trade
(C) China saw itself as the civilized center to which foreign rulers submitted
(D) The court was unaware Britain existed

questions.stem: Both the Ming dynasty and the Tokugawa shogunate permitted limited, regulated foreign trade — at Canton and Nagasaki respectively — rather than banning it outright. What does this similarity best illustrate?
options: (A) Both embraced unrestricted free trade with Europeans
(B) Both were conquered and colonized by European powers in the 1800s
(C) State-controlled trade that screened out foreign influence
(D) Both imposed a total ban on all foreign contact

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of the Turkish Letters (1555-1562), by a Flemish diplomat serving the Austrian emperor at the Ottoman court: No man owes his position to anything but valor and merit. The sultan carefully examines the character, ability, and disposition of candidates for promotion; men rise by merit, so posts go only to the competent, and this is why the Ottomans succeed in their undertakings and daily extend their empire. Among Austrians, by contrast, birth alone opens the door to public office. On campaign the sultan brings vast trains of camels and mules loaded with grain, knowing his armies must retreat across lands stripped bare; rations are weighed out daily, just enough to sustain life, to the Janissaries and royal troops. It is the patience, self-denial, and thrift of the Turkish soldier that lets him endure the worst conditions, a stark contrast to Christian soldiers who demand dainty dishes and mutiny without them. The sons of a sultan live in peril: on succession, the new sultan must kill his brothers, for the Janissaries will always demand largesses, and if refused, cry 'Long live the brother!' as a hint to enthrone a rival.
questions.stem: The passage praises Ottoman promotion by merit. Where did many of these merit-promoted officials come from?
options: (A) They were all Turkish nobles
(B) They were elected by popular vote of the empire's subjects in open, competitive contests
(C) Many were devshirme recruits: Christian boys trained for imperial service
(D) They purchased their offices

questions.stimulus: To the ruler of Persia. The learned doctors of our faith, both those who reason from the law and those who follow tradition, are agreed that the extirpation of heresy is a duty laid upon the faithful. Your followers have abandoned the true path, seducing the believers of our eastern provinces with false doctrines and raising rebellion against rightful authority. The Prophet himself commanded that innovators be driven out. We have therefore resolved, after long patience, to take up arms, not from ambition, but in obedience to the divine command that error be rooted out wherever it appears. Prepare yourself, for we march against you. Selim, Sultan of the Ottomans, 1514.
questions.stem: The Safavid Empire differed from its Ottoman and Mughal contemporaries most significantly in
options: (A) Its rejection of gunpowder weapons
(B) Its location in the Western Hemisphere across the ocean
(C) Its adoption of Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion
(D) Its lack of any centralized bureaucracy or administration

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Robert K. Massie's account of Peter the Great: In Protestant Europe Peter saw constitutions, bills of rights, and parliaments embodying new civil and political rights, yet he returned to Russia with no intention of sharing power. On the contrary, he was convinced that Russia's transformation required his own direction and driving force. He would lead, and where education and persuasion failed, he would drive and if necessary flog the backward nation forward.
questions.stem: Peter westernized the army, administration, and culture, yet kept and extended serfdom. Why didn't his reforms touch serfdom?
options: (A) He forgot about the serfs amid his many other reform projects
(B) The army and treasury depended on serf labor and taxes
(C) The serfs were already free
(D) No European country had serfdom

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of an account by a German mercenary who joined a Spanish expedition to South America in 1535 and was present at the founding of Asuncion, Paraguay, in 1537: The town of Lampere had dug pits lined with sharpened stakes to trap pursuing Christians. When our commander gathered his soldiers — no more than three hundred — and marched on Lampere, its people, who had learned of our coming, assembled an army of four thousand with bows and arrows in their fashion. They sent word offering to supply us with food and necessities if we would peacefully return to our companions. But it suited neither our commander nor ourselves to accept, for this nation and country, with its abundance of provisions, was most convenient for us — especially since in four whole years we had not seen a morsel of bread, living only on fish and flesh, and often in great scarcity. We replied that they should keep quiet and we would be their friends. They refused. Then we fired our brass guns at them. Hearing and seeing so many fall dead, with neither bullets nor arrows visible but only holes in their bodies, they fled in terror to shelter in their town, and more than three hundred, in their panic, fell into the very pits they had dug. We then assaulted the town, which they defended courageously for three days.
questions.stem: A child of a Spanish commander and a Native American woman was classified as mestizo, ranked below Spaniards but above natives. What principle organized this hierarchy?
options: (A) Personal wealth alone, regardless of ancestry or birthplace
(B) Proximity to Spanish birth and ancestry
(C) Depth of religious devotion
(D) Military rank achieved

questions.stimulus: The workingman's true grievance is not low wages but insecurity. He cannot be certain of keeping his employment from one year to the next; he cannot be certain of his health; and he knows that old age will one day rob him of the power to earn his bread. Should sickness or misfortune strike, he sinks into poverty, and society washes its hands of him. The ordinary poor-relief, especially in the great cities, is a disgrace. A man may have labored faithfully all his life, yet find himself helpless and abandoned. It is the duty of the state, therefore, to recognize an obligation toward those whose labor sustains it, and to provide by law for the sick, the injured, and the aged, lest desperation drive them into the arms of those who preach revolution.
questions.stem: The concerns described in the passage, insecurity about employment, health, and old age, reappeared throughout the twentieth century in debates over
options: (A) The exploration of outer space and the moon
(B) The abolition of currency and all forms of money
(C) The scope of government social-welfare programs
(D) The end of all industrial production worldwide

questions.stimulus:
The Uruguayan writer Eduardo Galeano opened his 1971 book 'Open Veins of Latin America' with a stark claim: 'The division of labor among nations is that some specialize in winning and others in losing. Our part of the world, known today as Latin America, was precocious: it has specialized in losing.'

Dependency theory emerged in the 1960s among Latin American economists — Raúl Prebisch at the UN Economic Commission for Latin America above all — who argued that the world economy was structured to enrich the industrial 'center' at the expense of the raw-material 'periphery.' Galeano's book was the theory's most passionate popular statement: a five-century indictment arguing that Latin America's poverty was not a stage of development but the product of development elsewhere.
questions.stem: Galeano's argument belongs to which school of thought?
options: (A) Dependency theory
(B) Modernization theory, blaming internal backwardness
(C) Fascism, glorifying the authoritarian state
(D) Isolationism, avoiding foreign entanglements

questions.stimulus:
...it is not unreasonable to conclude that the Japanese and Korean peoples formed for a long time one and the same nation. The recent annexation of Korea by Japan is therefore not the incorporation of two different countries inhabited by different races, but, it may rather be said to be the reunion of two sections of the one and same nation after a long period of separation. Indeed it is nothing more nor less than the old state of things restored.... In developing the industry of an infantile nation, it is advisable to begin the work by undertaking the improvement of the agricultural industry, and this has been diligently carried on since Japan assumed the protectorate of the Korean Empire.

Source: Komatsu Midori, 'The Old People and the New Government,' in Transactions of the Korea Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1912
questions.stem: The author's reference to developing the industry of an 'infantile nation' most clearly reflects which of the following ideologies?
options: (A) The passage advocates Korean self-government and national independence from Japan.
(B) Japan sought to preserve Korea's traditional agrarian economy unchanged.
(C) Imperial powers justified domination by portraying colonized peoples as backward.
(D) The author opposed any Japanese expansion on the Asian mainland.

questions.stem: Why did Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika fail to save the Soviet Union?
options: (A) They abolished the Communist Party's leading role in 1986
(B) Unleashed criticism and half-measures that wrecked the planned economy
(C) They returned the USSR to full Stalinist central planning and censorship
(D) They severed all Soviet trade with Eastern Europe

questions.stimulus: We are neither Indians nor Europeans, but a species in between the legitimate proprietors of the country and the Spanish usurpers. Americans by birth and Europeans by law, we find ourselves engaged in a dual conflict: we dispute with the natives for titles of ownership, and at the same time we are struggling to maintain ourselves in the country that gave us birth against the opposition of the invaders. — Simón Bolívar, Jamaica Letter, 1815 (paraphrased)
questions.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Bolívar's claim that American-born Spaniards occupied a distinct, in-between position?
options: (A) Creoles led the independence armies because they wanted to restore the Indigenous empires and return all colonial land to Indigenous communities
(B) Spain granted American-born Spaniards equal representation in the Cortes of Cádiz
(C) Enslaved Africans in Spanish America were freed by Bolívar before the wars began
(D) the highest colonial offices were reserved for peninsulares born in Spain, while wealthy creoles were shut out of top power

questions.stimulus: Line chart titled 'Trade as a share of global GDP.' The line rises from about 25 percent around 1970 to about 60 percent in 2008, dips sharply in 2009, then recovers and climbs to about 62 percent by 2024. Subtitle: 'Sum of exports and imports of goods and services globally, divided by gross domestic product, expressed as a percentage.' Note below: 'Data source: World Bank (2024).'
questions.stem: A historian argues that institutions created after World War II laid the groundwork for the trend shown. Which evidence best supports that argument?
options: (A) the United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent future wars
(B) the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, an event that directly created the World Trade Organization and ended all tariffs worldwide
(C) successive GATT negotiating rounds and the creation of the WTO in 1995 steadily lowered tariff barriers
(D) the euro was introduced as a common European currency in 1999

questions.stimulus:
'Upon their arrival they were honorably and graciously received by the grand Khan, in a full assembly of his principal officers. When they drew nigh to his person, they paid their respects by prostrating themselves on the floor. He immediately commanded them to rise, and to relate to him the circumstances of their travels. The letters and the presents from the pope were then laid before him, and he bestowed much commendation on the fidelity of his ambassadors; receiving with due reverence the oil from the holy sepulchre, he gave directions that it should be preserved with religious care. Upon his observing Marco Polo, Nicolo made answer, This is your servant, and my son; upon which the grand Khan replied, He is welcome, and it pleases me much, and he caused him to be enrolled amongst his attendants of honor. And as long as the said brothers and Marco remained in the court of the grand Khan, they were honored even above his own courtiers. Marco learnt in a short time and adopted the manners of the Tartars, and acquired a proficiency in four different languages.'

Source: Marco Polo's Travels, circa 1300
questions.stem: Kublai Khan's reception of the Polos, including enrolling Marco among his attendants of honor, best illustrates which of the following Mongol practices?
options: (A) The Mongol court recruited talented foreigners into imperial service.
(B) The Mongols refused to employ non-Mongols in any official administrative capacity.
(C) The Polos were imprisoned upon arriving at the Mongol court.
(D) Kublai Khan rejected the pope's gifts with open contempt.

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Toussaint L'Ouverture's 1797 report to the French Directory, recounting his conversation with Commissioner Sonthonax: Sonthonax tells Toussaint, the colony's black inhabitants fear for their freedom, and the suspicious white colonists must all be slaughtered; everything is ready, needing only Toussaint's agreement. Toussaint reacts with disbelief. The next morning Sonthonax returns to the scheme, saying they are perfectly placed to act and that Toussaint's influence over the people makes him the ideal partner. Toussaint accuses him of trying to ruin him: killing the whites, seizing independence, after promising never to raise such projects again. Sonthonax backtracks, claiming he only means expulsion, not murder, but Toussaint notes the contradiction and warns that any white death would be blamed on him. Sonthonax swears never to speak of it again and begs Toussaint to keep the secret from his own officers. Toussaint coldly gives his word and takes his leave.
questions.stem: Toussaint wrote this report to the French Directory about his own loyalty and Sonthonax's treachery. What should historians consider when using it?
options: (A) The report is self-serving: Toussaint had reason to paint himself as loyal
(B) The report is perfectly objective
(C) Toussaint was illiterate
(D) The Directory could not read French and relied entirely on translators for all reports

questions.stimulus: One economist argues that an effective strategy for encouraging democracy is the spread of markets. Another adds that globalization and free trade spur economic growth and bring lower prices on many goods.
questions.stem: Both speakers praise free trade and open markets. Which policy would both most likely support?
options: (A) Nationalizing oil industries
(B) Reducing tariffs between nations
(C) Imposing strict import quotas
(D) Fixing prices by government decree

questions.stimulus: On the island called Hispana there are very lofty and beautiful mountains, rich farms, groves, and fields, most fertile both for cultivation and for pasturage, and well suited for building. The harbors of this island, and the excellence of its rivers in volume and wholesomeness, surpass human belief unless one sees them. Its trees, pasturelands, and fruits differ greatly from those of Juana. Moreover, this Hispana abounds in various kinds of spices, gold, and metals. The inhabitants, as I said before, are unprovided with any sort of iron; they are destitute of arms, which are entirely unknown to them and unsuited to them — not on account of any bodily deformity, for they are well made, but because they are timid and full of terror. — Christopher Columbus, report of his first voyage, 1493
questions.stem: Columbus's description of the islanders as 'destitute of arms' and 'timid and full of terror' most directly foreshadows which of the following?
options: (A) Spanish arguments that conquest would be easy because the native population could not resist.
(B) Spanish adoption of native Caribbean military tactics.
(C) Columbus's secret plan to arm the islanders as military allies in a future war against the rival Portuguese.
(D) A Spanish decision to avoid the island entirely.

questions.stimulus: Shared stimulus for items 014-016. Map titled 'Spread of the Black Death in Europe, 1346-1353.' Color bands with dates show the plague's advance year by year: 1346 in the Crimea and the Levant; 1347 in Constantinople, Alexandria, and the eastern Mediterranean; 1348 across Italy, France, and Spain; 1349 in England and Germany; 1350-1353 across Scandinavia, Russia, and Eastern Europe. White arrows mark land and maritime trade routes.
questions.stem: The pattern shown on the map best supports which of the following connections between trade and disease?
options: (A) Disease spread only where trade was absent, since isolated peoples lacked immunity.
(B) The plague traveled from Europe into Asia, moving in the opposite direction from the flow of Silk Road commerce and reaching China last of all.
(C) Land routes spread the plague, but the sea routes were left completely untouched.
(D) The same networks that moved silk, spices, and paper also moved pathogens, so commercial integration exposed the whole region to pandemic.

questions.stimulus: French print, 1789: 'The Third Estate carrying the clergy and nobility.' A bent peasant figure, labeled the Third Estate, staggers under the weight of a plump clergyman (First Estate) riding on his back alongside a sword-bearing nobleman (Second Estate); the peasant groans while the two riders look comfortable. Chains and tax papers litter the ground.
questions.stem: A historian claims that France's fiscal crisis — not only Enlightenment ideas — drove the Revolution. Which evidence best supports this claim?
options: (A) Philosophes' books were bestsellers among Parisian lawyers
(B) Napoleon later built a large empire across Europe
(C) The monarchy was bankrupt from war debts, above all the American war, while the First and Second Estates paid almost no taxes
(D) The Third Estate cartoon by itself proves that Enlightenment ideas alone caused the Revolution, making any fiscal explanation unnecessary

questions.stimulus: Critics of Copernicus argued that the Bible says the sun moves and the earth stands still, and that since the Bible cannot err, heliocentrism must be heresy. Galileo replied that the Bible never speaks untruth when its true meaning is understood, but that its words are often abstruse and say things quite different from what their bare wording seems to signify. (Paraphrased from Galileo Galilei's letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany, 1615.)
questions.stem: The outcome of Galileo's trial best illustrates
options: (A) the limits religious institutions could place on new ideas in early modern Europe
(B) the complete triumph and vindication of heliocentrism by the Catholic Church in 1633
(C) widespread popular support for the Inquisition
(D) the end of all astronomical research in Europe

questions.stimulus:
'The question as to who, and what, is responsible for African underdevelopment can be answered at two levels. Firstly, the answer is that the operation of the imperialist system bears major responsibility for African economic retardation by draining African wealth and by making it impossible to develop more rapidly the resources of the continent. Secondly, one has to deal with those who manipulate the system and those who are either agents or unwitting accomplices of the said system. The capitalists of Western Europe were the ones who actively extended their exploitation from inside Europe to cover the whole of Africa.'

Source: Walter Rodney, historian, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa, 1974
questions.stem: The relationship between the firearms trade and the slave trade in West Africa is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) Firearms reduced the level of warfare in West Africa.
(B) The trade in guns and captives was equal and mutually beneficial.
(C) African states had no interest in European firearms.
(D) Needing guns to capture slaves to buy more guns created a cycle.

questions.stimulus: Two trading city-states, c. 1300: Venice, at the head of the Adriatic, grew rich carrying Eastern spices and silks into Europe in its galleys, and its merchants financed voyages with sea-loans. Kilwa, on the Swahili coast, grew rich carrying Arabian cloth and Indian porcelain into Africa in its dhows, exchanging them for interior gold.
questions.stem: Which of the following comparisons between Venice and Kilwa is best supported by the description?
options: (A) Both cities depended chiefly on overland camel caravans crossing the deserts and steppes of the interior, rather than on any ships at all, for their prosperity.
(B) Venice used its navy to dominate and control Kilwa's commerce.
(C) Both thrived as middlemen linking producers and buyers across regions, with ships and credit fitted to their own seas.
(D) Kilwa grew rich by manufacturing goods while Venice lived by farming alone.

questions.stimulus:
'At the beginning of the new year the rulers of each village came to Cuzco, bringing their quipus, which told how many births there had been during the year, and how many deaths. In this way the Inca and the governors knew which of the Indians were poor, the women who had been widowed, whether they were able to pay their taxes, and how many men they could count on in the event of war, and many other things they considered highly important. The Incas took care to see that justice was meted out, so much so that nobody ventured to commit a felony or theft.'

Source: Pedro de Cieza de Leon's Chronicles of the Incas (1540)
questions.stem: The Inca Empire's rapid expansion across the Andes in the fifteenth century is best explained by which of the following?
options: (A) The Inca relied on gunpowder weapons for their conquests.
(B) The Inca expanded exclusively through peaceful trade.
(C) The Inca had no system for administering conquered peoples.
(D) The Inca combined military conquest with administrative integration of new territories.

questions.stimulus: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains,' wrote Jean-Jacques Rousseau in The Social Contract (1762). 'Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will' — so that legitimate government rests on the people's collective will, not on kings or tradition.
questions.stem: Rousseau's purpose in writing The Social Contract was most likely to:
options: (A) defend the divine right of absolute monarchs
(B) argue that legitimate political authority comes from the people's general will, challenging existing governments
(C) serve as an official instruction manual for French royal administrators directly governing the provinces on the king's behalf
(D) organize factory workers into trade unions

questions.stimulus: From 'Ever Higher' (1920), an anthem of the early Soviet air force, by Pavel German and Julius Khait: 'We were born to make fairy tales come true, to overcome distance and space. Our reason has given steel wings to our hands, and throbbing motors in place of our hearts. Ever higher, higher and higher we speed the flight of our birds, and in every propeller breathes the tranquility of our borders. ... We feel our air force growing stronger — our workers' air force, the first in the world.'
questions.stem: Calling the air force 'our workers' air force' was significant mainly because it
options: (A) Tied military strength to the regime's claim to represent the working class
(B) Proved that workers had designed the airplanes themselves
(C) Showed that the anthem's authors opposed the government
(D) Promised that workers would control the military directly through elected soldiers' councils

questions.stimulus: President Woodrow Wilson, address to Congress, January 8, 1918: 'A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.'
questions.stem: Wilson's primary purpose in proposing this 'general association of nations' was to:
options: (A) Build a permanent military alliance directed against Germany after the war
(B) Convince Americans and Allied leaders that the war was fought for a democratic, rule-based peace
(C) Demand Germany's immediate and unconditional surrender to the Allies
(D) Win the United States a permanent seat alongside Britain and France on their joint imperial war councils

questions.stimulus: Paraphrase of Ruben Dario's 1904 poem 'To Roosevelt': You are the United States, the future invader of the native America that has Indian blood, that still prays to Jesus Christ and still speaks Spanish. You think life is fire and progress is eruption, that wherever you aim you strike the future. But our America has had poets since the ancient days of Netzahualcoyotl, has consulted the stars, has lived on light and love since remote times, the America of Montezuma and the Inca, Catholic and Spanish America. It lives, and it dreams, and it loves. Be careful: a thousand cubs of the Spanish lion are loosed. To seize us in your iron claws, Roosevelt, you would need to be God's own hunter. And though you count on everything, you lack one thing: God.
questions.stem: The poem warns Roosevelt that 'a thousand cubs' of the Spanish lion are loosed. What is Dario predicting?

questions.stimulus:
'The Romanists have, with great adroitness, drawn three walls round themselves, with which they have hitherto protected themselves, so that no one could reform them, whereby all Christendom has fallen terribly. Firstly, if pressed by the temporal power, they have affirmed that the temporal power has no jurisdiction over them, but that the spiritual power is above the temporal. Secondly, if it were proposed to admonish them with the Scriptures, they objected that no one may interpret the Scriptures but the Pope. Thirdly, if they are threatened with a council, they pretend that no one may call a council but the Pope.

The second wall is even more tottering and weak: that they alone pretend to be considered masters of the Scriptures. They assume authority, saying that the Pope cannot err in matters of faith, whether he be evil or good, albeit they cannot prove it by a single letter. Source: Martin Luther, Address to the Nobility of the German Nation, 1520

questions.stimulus:
Olympe de Gouges, author of the 1791 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman,' was arrested during the Terror and sent to the guillotine in November 1793 — one of a number of outspoken women silenced as the revolution turned against its own.

Her real offense was political, not literary. De Gouges had attacked Robespierre and the Montagnards, defended the Girondins, and — fatally — proposed a plebiscite on the form of government, which the revolutionary tribunal read as royalism. At her trial she was denied a lawyer. The Terror devoured its critics indiscriminately, but women who entered politics faced an additional charge simply for speaking in public at all.

questions.stimulus: "If I were to record the services I have rendered the French government, I should need many volumes. As a reward, I have been arbitrarily arrested at St. Domingo, bound, and put on board ship like a criminal, without regard for my rank. I was once worth 648,000 francs; I spent it in the service of my country. Today they seek to cover me with opprobrium and infamy. I am made the most unhappy of men: my liberty is taken from me, and I am separated from my aged father, my wife, and my children." - Toussaint L'Ouverture, memoirs written in a French prison, 1802. Context: L'Ouverture, a formerly enslaved man, led the revolution in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. questions.stimulus: When the Portuguese sail from Macao in China to Japan, they carry much white silk, gold, musk, and porcelain, and they bring back from Japan nothing but silver. A great carrack goes there every year and returns with some six hundred thousand coins' worth of silver; and all this Japanese silver, together with another two hundred thousand coins' worth brought yearly out of India, they employ to great advantage in China, carrying away gold, musk, silk, copper, porcelain, and many other costly and gilded things. When the Portuguese come to Canton to trade, they may remain only a set number of days: on entering the city gate they must write their names in a book, and on going out at night they must strike them out. questions.stimulus:
An Arab chronicler writing around 1220 described the Mongol invasion of the Islamic world as a calamity unlike any other: the invaders, he wrote, spared neither women nor children, and their deeds 'horrify all who hear of them.' He presented the invasion as a catastrophe visited upon Islam and its peoples, and could barely bring himself to record what had happened.

The devastation he describes fell hardest on the cities of Persia and Central Asia — Merv, Nishapur, Herat — whose artisans were killed or enslaved and whose irrigation works were wrecked. Yet within a generation, Mongol rulers were rebuilding many of these same cities as administrative centers: sponsoring observatories and workshops, repairing canals, and guaranteeing the safety of merchants on the overland routes. The chronicler, writing at the moment of destruction, could not see the reconstruction that followed.
questions.stem: A historian studying the revival of long-distance Eurasian trade in the later 1200s would most reasonably treat this passage as
options: (A) evidence that contemporary observers welcomed the Mongols as restorers of order
(B) the best available record of the volume of goods traded along the Silk Road
(C) direct proof that Mongol conquests made all Eurasian trade impossible for the rest of the century
(D) vivid evidence of the violence of the initial conquests, but a limited guide to how Mongol rulers later treated merchants

questions.stimulus:
'Article 1: The Parties undertake, as set forth in the Charter of the United Nations, to settle any international dispute by peaceful means and to refrain from the threat or use of force inconsistent with the purposes of the United Nations.

Article 3: The Parties, separately and jointly, by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid, will maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack.

Article 5: The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all, and each of them will assist the Party so attacked by taking such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain security.'

questions.stimulus: In recent years the spontaneous forces of capitalism have steadily grown in our countryside: new rich peasants spring up everywhere, and many well-to-do middle peasants strive to become rich peasants. Meanwhile many poor peasants still live in poverty for lack of sufficient means of production, some in debt and others selling or renting out their land. If this tendency goes unchecked, the polarization of the countryside will inevitably grow worse day by day. The peasants who lose their land and those who remain in poverty will complain that we do nothing to save them from ruin; nor will the well-to-do middle peasants heading down the capitalist road be pleased with us, for we can never satisfy their demands unless we take the capitalist road ourselves. Can the worker-peasant alliance continue to stand in these circumstances? Obviously not. There is no solution except on a new basis: to bring about, step by step, the socialist transformation of the whole of agriculture, together with socialist industrialization and the socialist transformation of handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce — in other words, to carry out cooperation and eliminate the rich-peasant economy and the individual economy in the countryside, so that all rural people grow well-off together. This alone will consolidate the worker-peasant alliance. — Mao Zedong, On the Question of Agricultural Cooperation, 1955

questions.stimulus:
A 17th-century Japanese manual for merchants urges readers to live honestly, honor their parents and relatives, treat everyone with courtesy, avoid selfishness, and never lie. It presents commerce as an activity that must be conducted within strict moral bounds, warning that profit pursued without virtue brings disgrace.

The hierarchy was borrowed from Confucian thought, which ranked occupations by their contribution to society: samurai, who governed, first; then peasants, who grew the food; then artisans, who made things; and last the merchants, who merely moved goods about for profit. In practice, Tokugawa Japan's long peace made merchants indispensable — samurai stipends paid in rice had to be converted to cash, and the great merchant houses of Osaka became the bankers of the warrior class — but the formal ranking never changed, whatever the balance of wealth.
questions.stem: The social order assumed by the passage is best described as
options: (A) an egalitarian society with no formal ranks
(B) A Confucian hierarchy of samurai, peasants, artisans, merchants
(C) a feudal order based solely on who owned the most land overall
(D) a caste system determined entirely by ritual purity

His glasnost (openness) allowed freer speech and a freer press; his perestroika (restructuring) introduced limited private enterprise to revive a stagnant economy. The reforms were meant to strengthen socialism. Instead, newly free media exposed decades of failure, and nationalist movements in the Baltic republics and Central Asia demanded independence. section_1b.directions: Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (a, b, and c). You have 40 minutes for this section.

q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE effect of Sputnik on the United States according to the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the intense superpower competition in space.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity between the Space Race and earlier forms of great-power rivalry.

sample_answers.a: Sputnik panicked the United States into creating NASA and massively expanding science education and research funding to catch up with the Soviets.
sample_answers.b: One cause was that rockets were dual-use technology: the same missiles that could deliver nuclear warheads could launch satellites, so space achievements directly advertised military capability.
sample_answers.c: Like the nineteenth-century naval arms race, the Space Race was a prestige competition in which great powers measured themselves by mastery of the newest technology — battleships then, moon rockets now.

q1.stimulus: The Space Race was the Cold War's most spectacular proxy battle: Sputnik's beep in 1957 panicked Americans into creating NASA and pouring money into science education; Kennedy's 1961 pledge to reach the Moon committed the United States to the most expensive peacetime project in history. The rockets were built to carry warheads, but the contest was fought for prestige — each launch advertised which system could master the future. Apollo 11's landing in 1969 was a human triumph staged as an ideological victory.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from President John F. Kennedy, address at Rice University, September 12, 1962
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE goal Kennedy sets in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the speech reflects Cold War competition.
parts.c: Explain ONE domestic effect of the Apollo program in the United States.

sample_answers.a: Kennedy sets the goal of landing an American on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before 1970.
sample_answers.b: The speech frames the Moon landing as a contest with the Soviet Union — a peaceful arena in which to prove the superiority of the American system without fighting a war.
sample_answers.c: One domestic effect was a boom in science and engineering education and in high-tech industry: federal spending created new university research programs, new companies, and spinoff technologies from integrated circuits to medical imaging.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of Kennedy's speech:] We choose to go to the Moon in this decade — not because it is easy, but because it is hard. This challenge will test our science, our industry, and our determination, and it will show the world what free men can achieve.

q3.attribution: NASA photograph of Buzz Aldrin on the Moon, Apollo 11, July 20, 1969
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE detail of the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the photograph served American Cold War goals.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the Space Race changed international cooperation after 1969.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows an astronaut in a bulky white spacesuit standing on gray lunar soil beside the American flag, with the black sky and the lunar module behind him.
sample_answers.b: The image — an American flag planted on another world, broadcast live to hundreds of millions of people — was the ultimate prestige victory, visually proving American technological supremacy over the Soviet Union.
sample_answers.c: After the race was won, rivalry gave way to cooperation: the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz docking and later the International Space Station showed space shifting from a contest to a joint project.

q3.stimulus: NASA photograph of Buzz Aldrin on the surface of the Moon, July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission — an astronaut beside the deployed American flag with the lunar module in the background.

q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the causes of accelerated globalization after 1980
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE cause of accelerated globalization described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE effect of containerization on world trade.
parts.c: Explain ONE way globalization after 1980 differed from the first wave of globalization before 1914.

sample_answers.a: One cause was the shipping container, which standardized cargo handling and cut the cost of moving goods by sea dramatically.
sample_answers.b: Containerization made long-distance shipping so cheap that firms could split manufacturing across continents — making parts wherever labor or materials were cheapest and assembling elsewhere — creating global supply chains.
sample_answers.c: The pre-1914 wave moved mainly raw materials and migrants under colonial empires, while the post-1980 wave moved manufactured components through supply chains managed by multinational firms, with production fragmented across many countries rather than concentrated in one.

q1.stimulus: Globalization after 1980 was built on three revolutions: the container, which cut shipping costs by an order of magnitude; the microchip, which let firms coordinate production across continents in real time; and policy, as China, India, and the former Soviet bloc opened to world markets. The result was the great supply chain: designed in California, assembled in Shenzhen, sold in Berlin. For the first time, a single product's manufacture routinely spanned a dozen countries.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Deng Xiaoping, remarks during his Southern Tour of China, 1992
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE policy Deng advocates in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of Deng's 1992 push for deeper reform.
parts.c: Explain ONE effect of China's opening on the global economy.

sample_answers.a: Deng advocates deepening market reforms and further opening China to foreign trade and investment.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the conservative backlash after 1989, which had stalled reform; Deng's tour was a political intervention to restart marketization and reassure investors that opening would continue.
sample_answers.c: One effect was China's rise as the 'world's factory': hundreds of millions of workers entered global manufacturing, lowering consumer prices worldwide while hollowing out industrial employment in rich countries.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of Deng's remarks:] China must deepen its market reforms and open still further to the outside world. Development is the only hard truth. Poverty is not socialism — whoever stands in the way of reform will be left behind.

q3.attribution: Photograph of a modern container ship
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the ship shown in the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE way container ships illustrate the mechanisms of globalization.
parts.c: Explain ONE environmental cost of the shipping system shown in the photograph.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows a gigantic vessel stacked many containers high and deep with identical steel boxes — cargo as pure standardized volume.
sample_answers.b: The ship embodies globalization's logic: standardized containers move seamlessly from ship to truck to train, making it economical to manufacture goods across a dozen countries and assemble them in another.
sample_answers.c: One cost is emissions: container ships burn heavy bunker fuel, making international shipping a major source of carbon dioxide and sulfur pollution — the hidden environmental price of cheap global goods.

q3.stimulus: Photograph of a modern container ship loaded with thousands of standardized steel containers — the workhorse of global trade.

q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the digital revolution and globalization since 1990
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way the internet changed global commerce according to the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the internet's rapid global spread after 1990.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity between the digital revolution and earlier communications revolutions such as print.

sample_answers.a: The internet made services tradable across distance — programmers, call-center workers, and designers in Asia and Latin America could sell directly to clients in rich countries.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the convergence of cheap computing, fiber-optic cables, and the World Wide Web's open standards, which together collapsed the cost of transmitting information to near zero.
sample_answers.c: Like the printing press, the internet decentralized the production of information and challenged established gatekeepers — printers defied the Church's monopoly on texts as bloggers and social media defied state and corporate media monopolies.

q1.stimulus: The internet did to services what the container did to goods: it made them tradable across distance. A programmer in Bangalore, a call-center worker in Manila, and a designer in São Paulo could now sell directly to clients in London or New York. Information that once required a library, a newspaper, or a stockbroker now arrived instantly and nearly free. But the same networks that spread knowledge also spread misinformation, surveillance, and cyberwarfare — the digital revolution, like every communications revolution before it, empowered both liberation and control.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from the United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report, 1999
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE concern the report raises.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the digital divide described in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the digital divide has changed since 1999.

sample_answers.a: The report warns that information technology's benefits are concentrating in rich countries while most of humanity remains unconnected, threatening to widen global inequality.
sample_answers.b: One cause was infrastructure cost: building phone and internet networks required capital, electricity, and literacy that poor regions lacked, so investment flowed where returns were surest.
sample_answers.c: Mobile phones have narrowed the access gap dramatically — billions now carry internet-connected phones — though gaps in speed, affordability, and digital skills persist between rich and poor regions.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of the report's argument:] The new information technologies are concentrating their benefits in the wealthy countries. While the internet connects millions, most of humanity has never made a telephone call. Unless access spreads, the digital divide will widen the gap between rich and poor nations.

q3.attribution: The Opte Project's visualization of global internet connections, 2005
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown in the image.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the image illustrates globalization.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of the image as evidence about who benefits from the internet.

sample_answers.a: The image shows dense clusters of connections in North America, Europe, and East Asia, with far sparser links across Africa and parts of South Asia — a visibly uneven network.
sample_answers.b: The image makes globalization tangible: it shows a single physical infrastructure binding continents together, the material base of the instant communication and commerce described in the passages.
sample_answers.c: The image shows connections, not users or uses — a glowing node might be a server farm, and the map cannot show who is excluded, what the network is used for, or who controls it.

q3.stimulus: The Opte Project's visualization of internet connections around the world (2005): glowing nodes and links mapping the physical structure of the global internet, released under a Creative Commons license.

section_2a.directions: Question 1 is based on the accompanying documents. The documents have been edited for the purpose of this exercise. You are advised to spend 15 minutes reading and planning and 45 minutes writing your answer.

dbq.analysis_note: All documents are paraphrased or original summaries; no extended quotation of copyrighted sources.

documents.source_line: Summary of the Tennessee Valley Authority Act's stated purposes (original treatment)
documents.sourcing_note: An original summary of the legislation's public aims; purpose of the act was regional uplift. Its language of progress and planning represents the pro-dam case at its most idealistic.
documents.text_or_description: The TVA was created to tame the floods of the Tennessee River, generate cheap electricity, and lift one of America's poorest regions out of poverty through planned development — a promise that government engineering could remake both nature and society.

documents.source_line: Summary of a U.S. Bureau of Reclamation statement on the Hoover (Boulder) Dam project (original treatment)
documents.sourcing_note: An original summary of the builder's case; purpose is to justify a massive public expenditure during the Depression. Jobs, water, and power are the classic benefits claimed for big dams.
documents.text_or_description: The dam would put thousands of unemployed men to work, store the Colorado River's floods, and deliver water and electricity to farms and cities across the Southwest — turning a desert waste into productive land.

documents.source_line: Paraphrased account of Nubian families displaced by the Aswan High Dam, Egypt
documents.sourcing_note: A paraphrase of displaced people's testimonies collected by journalists and scholars; purpose is to record the human cost. Those who lost ancestral villages experienced the dam as catastrophe, not progress.
documents.text_or_description: We were taken from the villages where our grandfathers are buried and settled in desert lands we did not know. The government promised new houses and fields, but the soil was poor and the water far. The lake swallowed our date palms and our history.

documents.source_line: Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister of India, on large dams (paraphrased)
documents.sourcing_note: India's leader speaking to his nation; purpose is to inspire faith in modernization. His famous 'temples' language shows how dams became symbols of post-colonial national pride, not just engineering.
documents.text_or_description: Nehru called great dams the temples of modern India, monuments to the nation's resolve to conquer poverty through science and planning. To build them was an act of patriotism; to question them, near disloyalty.

documents.source_line: Findings of the World Commission on Dams (paraphrased)
documents.sourcing_note: An independent international commission reviewing the global record; purpose is assessment, not advocacy. Its numbers gave critics authoritative evidence after decades of anecdote.
documents.text_or_description: The Commission found that large dams had displaced some 40 to 80 million people worldwide, that their electricity and irrigation benefits often fell short of projections, and that the poorest communities bore the costs while distant cities reaped the power.

documents.license: Public domain (U.S. federal government work, Wikimedia Commons)
documents.source_line: Aerial photograph of the Hoover Dam
documents.sourcing_note: A U.S. government photograph; purpose is to document and celebrate the achievement. The dam's sheer scale in a stark desert canyon visualizes both the engineering triumph and the audacity of reshaping a river.
documents.text_or_description: The aerial view shows the great curved concrete wall spanning Black Canyon, holding back the vast blue reservoir of Lake Mead amid bare desert mountains — human engineering imposed on an arid landscape.

documents.license: Public domain (U.S. federal government work; copyright not renewed)
documents.source_line: TVA diagram of its water-control system
documents.sourcing_note: A government planning diagram; purpose is to show mastery — every dam, reservoir, and channel in its place. The tidy schematic embodies the planner's faith that nature can be managed like a machine.
documents.text_or_description: The diagram maps the Tennessee Valley's chain of dams, reservoirs, and navigation channels as one integrated system, each structure labeled and linked — a portrait of a river entirely reorganized by human design.

dbq.prompt: Using the documents and your knowledge of world history, evaluate the extent to which large hydroelectric dam projects have benefited or harmed societies in the twentieth century.

analysis.complexity: Multiple paths: weigh benefits (electricity, flood control, jobs, national pride — Docs 1, 2, 4) against harms (displacement, ecological damage, unmet promises — Docs 3, 5); corroborate the pro-dam case across Docs 1, 2, and 4, then contrast with Docs 3 and 5; qualify by asking who benefited vs. who paid (urban consumers vs. displaced villagers); Docs 6 and 7 together show the scale that made both the benefits and harms so large.
analysis.sourcing: Doc 1 (purpose: legislation selling a vision); Doc 2 (audience: a Depression public desperate for jobs); Doc 3 (point of view: the displaced, recorded secondhand); Doc 4 (context: a new nation proving itself); Doc 5 (purpose: an independent audit, decades later).

rubric_map.contextualization: Situate big dams within 20th-century developmentalism: the New Deal's faith in planning, post-colonial nations' drive to industrialize, Cold War competition in foreign aid (U.S. vs. Soviet dam projects), and the rise of environmental movements questioning such projects by the 1970s-1990s.

evidence.describe: All seven describable; strongest: Docs 1, 2, 4 (the promise), Docs 3, 5 (the reckoning), Docs 6, 7 (the scale).
evidence.outside: Outside evidence: the Three Gorges Dam (over a million displaced); the Aral Sea disaster from Soviet irrigation; siltation and the Nile delta's erosion after Aswan; dam failures (Banqiao, 1975); the Narmada Bachao Andolan protest movement in India; rural electrification's effects on quality of life.
evidence.support: 'Benefited' line: Docs 1, 2, 4, 6, 7. 'Harmed' line: Docs 3, 5. Doc 5 (the Commission) is the strongest harm evidence because it aggregates the global record.

rubric_map.thesis: An arguable thesis takes a position on 'extent' with a line of reasoning, e.g., the sample below.

dbq.sample_thesis: Large hydroelectric dams benefited societies substantially by delivering electricity, flood control, and jobs on a scale no alternative could match in the twentieth century; however, the benefits came at a severe cost, because the displacement of tens of millions and the ecological damage fell on the poorest communities while the power flowed to distant cities, making the dams' legacy deeply unequal.
dbq.title: Hydroelectric Dams in the Twentieth Century

section_2b.directions: Answer the question below. You have 40 minutes.

leq.exam: AP World History: Modern, May 2027 (Fall 2026 CED) - single required prompt, 40 min, 15% of score
leq.process_note: New-format LEQ: the student chooses their own reasoning process and evidence. The target process above is a coverage tag for bank balance, not a constraint on the student.
leq.prompt: In the period c. 1450-c. 1750, expanding interregional trade brought peoples, goods, and beliefs into sustained contact across Afro-Eurasia and the Americas. Develop an argument that evaluates the extent to which interregional trade caused religious and cultural syncretism in this period. Your response may focus on any example(s) that support your argument. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

rubric_map.thesis_1: Presents a historically defensible thesis that responds to the prompt and establishes a line of reasoning.
rubric_map.contextualization_1: Describes a broader historical context relevant to the prompt. Acceptable context: the growth of the Indian Ocean, Atlantic, and trans-Saharan trade networks, European colonial expansion, or missionary activity accompanying commerce.
rubric_map.evidence_examples_1: Identifies at least two specific historical examples relevant to the argument. Acceptable examples: Sikhism, Vodou/Santeria in the Americas, blending of Catholic and indigenous practice in Mexico and the Andes, Sufi accommodation in South and Southeast Asia, Swahili Islamic culture.
rubric_map.evidence_supports_argument_1: Uses the examples to support the argument rather than merely listing or describing them. Examples must be tied to the claim that trade caused syncretism (or that contact through trade did not reliably produce it).
rubric_map.analysis_reasoning_1: Uses the targeted historical reasoning process to structure the argument. Causation: evaluates whether trade was the cause of syncretism and considers alternatives such as conquest, missionary policy, or state enforcement of orthodoxy.
rubric_map.analysis_complex_understanding_1: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the historical development: e.g., qualifies the argument by explaining nuance or contradiction, evaluates multiple perspectives, or connects the argument across themes or time periods.

leq.sample_thesis: Trade created the sustained contact from which syncretic traditions emerged, but contact alone did not determine the outcome: where states and religious authorities enforced orthodoxy or segregated communities, as in Spanish America or the Ottoman millet system, trade produced coexistence rather than blending.
leq.evidence_directions: Strong responses show both blending (Sikhism, Afro-Caribbean religions, Mexican folk Catholicism) and resistance to blending (Inquisition, anti-Christian edicts, millet separation). One-sided 'trade always blended cultures' answers miss the evaluation the prompt demands.
